title: HTTP gRPC GraphQL and messaging comparisons
concepts: A communication protocol is a contract for exchanging information across a boundary; choose it from the interaction shape, clients, network constraints, operational needs, and evolution strategy rather than popularity.

HTTP supplies shared request and response semantics across multiple wire versions. A resource-oriented HTTP API, an operation-oriented RPC API, and a client-shaped GraphQL API can all use HTTP while exposing different contracts.

gRPC defines named service methods and typed messages with generated client and server code. Its streaming call forms and HTTP/2 transport suit persistent service-to-service interactions, but browser support and intermediaries may require additional setup.

GraphQL defines a typed schema and operations for clients to select a response shape. GraphQL itself is transport-independent; serving it over HTTP adds a separate transport contract, and the current GraphQL-over-HTTP document is a working draft.

Messaging separates production from consumption in time and can support queues, fan-out, and event streams; delivery, ordering, retries, and broker behavior are treated in t08-008 rather than hidden inside an API comparison.
No protocol automatically supplies authorization, compatibility policy, observability, resource limits, or safe retries. Those concerns must be designed and tested at the boundary that owns them.

QUERY is a standardized safe and idempotent HTTP method whose request content is processed to produce a result; it can be repeated without partial state changes. Support and intermediary compatibility must be checked before adopting it.
Empty selection sets are valid, including the empty query form {}.
Directives may now annotate directive definitions using the DIRECTIVE_DEFINITION location, with cycles prohibited.
OneOf input-object inhabitability rules prevent recursively impossible OneOf definitions; do not imply @oneOf was introduced in 2026.

versionNotes.edition: GraphQL over HTTP, November 2026 Working Draft
items: A separate, current Working Draft specifies interoperability conventions for serving GraphQL over HTTP; it extends but does not replace the GraphQL language specification and is not a final released standard.
